For resale and securities borrowed agreements, the Firm is exposed to credit risk to the extent that the value of the securities received is less than the initial cash principal advanced and any collateral amounts exchanged [1]. For repurchase and securities loaned agreements, the exposure runs the other way: credit risk arises to the extent that the value of the underlying securities advanced exceeds the value of the initial cash principal received, and any collateral amounts exchanged [1]. To manage these risks, the Firm monitors the value of the underlying securities against the cash proceeds and exchanged collateral, requesting additional collateral or returning securities or collateral when appropriate [1]. It also typically enters into master netting agreements, which give it the right to liquidate the underlying securities and any collateral amounts exchanged if a counterparty defaults [1]. Because of these credit risk mitigation practices, the Firm did not hold any allowance for credit losses on resale and securities borrowed arrangements as of December 31, 2025 and 2024 [2].

In fiscal 2024, JPMorgan Chase said securities financing agreements expose the Firm primarily to credit and liquidity risk [1]. To manage these risks, it monitors the value of the underlying securities (predominantly high-quality securities collateral, including government-issued debt and U.S. GSEs and government agencies MBS) received from or provided to counterparties against the value of cash proceeds and exchanged collateral, and either requests additional collateral or returns securities or collateral when appropriate [1]. Margin levels are initially established based on the counterparty, the type of underlying securities, and the permissible collateral, and are monitored on an ongoing basis [1]. Credit exposure arises in resale and securities borrowed agreements to the extent the value of securities received is less than the initial cash principal advanced and any collateral exchanged, and in repurchase and securities loaned agreements to the extent the value of securities advanced exceeds the initial cash principal received and any collateral exchanged [1]. Protections in a counterparty default: the Firm typically enters into master netting agreements and similar arrangements that give the right to liquidate the underlying securities and any collateral amounts exchanged upon a counterparty default [1]. It is also the Firm's policy to take possession, where possible, of the securities underlying resale and securities borrowed agreements [1].

Purpose: JPMorgan uses credit derivatives, which primarily consist of CDS, to manage the counterparty credit risk associated with loans and lending-related commitments [8]. The Firm also uses credit derivatives and credit-related notes in credit portfolio management activities to manage loans and lending-related commitments ($9,899 million notional at December 31, 2025) and derivative receivables ($13,999 million), totaling $23,898 million (vs. $40,888 million in 2024) [4]. The Firm manages the credit risk on contracts to sell protection by purchasing protection with identical or similar underlying reference entities [3]. It also obtains credit protection against certain loans in the retained loan portfolio through the issuance of credit-related notes [1]. Hedge accounting: No. The credit derivatives used in credit portfolio management activities do not qualify for hedge accounting under U.S. GAAP [6]; they are reported at fair value, with gains and losses recognized in principal transactions revenue [6]. The Firm does not apply hedge accounting to purchased CDS used to manage the credit risk of loans and lending-related commitments, because of the difficulties in qualifying such contracts as hedges [5]. In contrast, the loans and lending-related commitments being risk-managed are accounted for on an accrual basis, and this asymmetry causes earnings volatility that the Firm views as not representative of the true changes in value of its overall credit exposure [6].

Alphabet's fiscal 2025 foreign currency risk disclosure uses a scenario assumption. Considering historical trends in foreign exchange rates, it determined that adverse changes in exchange rates of 10% were reasonably possible, and it ran a sensitivity analysis on its foreign currency exposures to estimate the impact of that adverse 10% change [4]. The fiscal 2025 table reports the resulting figures as of December 31, 2025, such as $671 million for foreign denominated monetary assets and liabilities (OI&E impact) [2]. The fiscal 2023 interest rate risk disclosure instead uses a statistical method, value-at-risk (VaR) analysis. VaR is the expected loss in fair value, for a given confidence interval, of the investment portfolio due to adverse movements in interest rates. Alphabet uses a variance/covariance VaR model with a 95% confidence interval, and it reports the estimated one-day loss in fair value of marketable debt securities [7]. In short, foreign currency risk is measured with a fixed 10% adverse-move scenario, while interest rate risk is measured with a 95% confidence, one-day VaR model.

Apple uses a hypothetical rate-shock (sensitivity) approach, while Alphabet uses a value-at-risk (VaR) model. Apple's fiscal 2023 disclosure sets out the potential impacts on its investment portfolio and term debt from a hypothetical increase in relevant interest rates as of September 30, 2023 and September 24, 2022 [5]. The table applies a 100 basis point increase across all tenors, with the impact on the investment portfolio shown as a decline in fair value of $3,089 (2023) versus $4,022 (2022), in millions. It also shows an increase in annual interest expense on term debt of $194 (2023) versus $201 (2022) [1]. Apple's figures include the effects of any associated derivatives [5]. Alphabet instead uses VaR analysis to determine the potential effect of interest rate fluctuations on its marketable debt security portfolio. The VaR is the expected loss in fair value, for a given confidence interval, due to adverse interest rate movements. It is calculated with a variance/covariance VaR model at a 95% confidence interval, and it estimates a one-day loss in fair value as of December 31, 2022 and 2023 [4]. Alphabet's table reports an interest rate risk category of $256 (2022) and $296 (2023) as of December 31, with 12-month averages of $198 (2022) and $271 (2023) [6]. The passages do not state units for the table itself, but the VaR text says amounts are in millions [4]. In short, Apple's measure is a fixed 100 bp shock covering both asset fair value and debt interest expense, while Alphabet's is a probabilistic one-day, 95%-confidence loss estimate on its debt securities portfolio.

FY2023 methodology: Alphabet uses VaR analysis to determine the potential effect of interest rate fluctuations on the value of its marketable debt security portfolio. VaR is the expected loss in fair value, for a given confidence interval, from adverse interest rate movements, using a variance/covariance VaR model with a 95% confidence interval; the one-day loss estimates were presented as of December 31, 2022 and 2023 [3]. The FY2023 risk category - interest rate figures were $256 million (2022) and $296 million (2023) at year-end, and 12-month averages of $198 million and $271 million [2] (the $ amounts are in millions per [3]). FY2025 comparison: the FY2025 filing describes the same approach, now applied to the 'investment portfolio' (rather than only 'marketable debt security portfolio'), with the same expected-loss definition and a variance/covariance model at 95% confidence [8]. Its caveat states that actual future gains and losses may differ materially from the sensitivity analyses as of December 31, 2024 and 2025, due to inherent limitations in predicting the timing and amount of interest rate changes and actual exposures and positions, and that VaR is not intended to represent actual losses but is used as a risk estimation [1]. (The FY2023 passages provided do not include a comparable caveat, so I cannot say whether one existed.) What FY2025 adds on senior unsecured notes: total carrying value of $11.9 billion and $48.5 billion as of December 31, 2024 and 2025; because they primarily bear fixed rates and are recorded at amortized cost, interest rate fluctuations generally do not affect the consolidated financial statements, though the fair value of the notes will fluctuate with market rates [1]. Of the $48.5 billion, $2.0 billion was short-term, with short-term and long-term future interest payments of $1.8 billion and $35.7 billion; during 2025 Alphabet issued $22.5 billion of US dollar-denominated and €13.25 billion of euro-denominated senior unsecured notes [5]. By contrast, the FY2023 passages describe the notes as fixed-rate with estimated fair value of about $10.3 billion at December 31, 2023 [7].

The two descriptions differ in the channel of impact. Amazon says its long-term debt is carried at amortized cost, so interest rate fluctuations do not impact its consolidated financial statements; the fair value of its fixed-rate long-term debt generally fluctuates with rates, declining in periods of increasing rates [1]. Amazon's debt as of December 31, 2023 had a face value of $67.2 billion, primarily fixed rate unsecured senior notes [3]. Apple, by contrast, says increases in interest rates will increase the interest expense on its term debt (and negatively affect the fair value of its investment portfolio) [2]. Apple also says it may use derivatives, offset interest rate–sensitive assets and liabilities, or control duration to protect against this risk [2], and quantifies the effect: a 100 basis point increase would raise annual interest expense on term debt by $194 million in 2023 (vs. $201 million in 2022) [6]. So Amazon frames rising rates as lowering the fair value of its fixed-rate debt with no financial statement impact, while Apple frames rising rates as raising its interest expense and gives a sensitivity figure [1][2][6]. The passages do not give an Amazon dollar sensitivity for its debt.
